GLEUHR Branch Manager Training Module
Oct 21, 2026 · @Gleuhr
How to use this module
This module turns every GLEUHR Branch Manager document into one teachable course: 9 framework modules in 3 streams, 2 administration modules from the September–October 2026 process guidelines, a Playbook lab, a 3-day solo Final Test, and a deployment meeting, delivered over 14 to 20 days at Chandigarh HQ.
Who uses it
The trainee BM reads each module the evening before it runs, completes the exercises, and keeps this document open as her reference after deployment.
The trainers (Jaspreet, Arshpreet, Saurabh, the Senior Therapist, Dr Kanikta, the Senior Doctor, the Senior Counsellor, Manisha, the Regional Head, Harman, and the Founder) use the lesson notes, exercises and sign-off criteria to run and score their module.
The Regional Head uses the Final Test and Deployment sections to decide readiness.
How each module is laid out
Why it matters: the reason the module exists, in one or two lines.
Learning outcomes: what the BM must be able to do by the end.
Lesson content: the standard itself, drawn from the SOP, Playbook and checklists.
Activities and exercises: day by day, with who runs them.
Sign-off: the competencies exactly as scored in the BM Training Tracker (0 = not yet, 1 = signed off). Sign-off requires evidence, not attendance.

The sign-off principle
Sign-off requires evidence of competence, plus a final readiness test. Attendance is not evidence.
Each trainer scores each competency 0 (not yet) or 1 (signed off) in the Training Tracker.
A module shows SIGNED OFF only when every competency scores 1.
Module 4 (Doctor Coordination) is the critical module. Spend the time here even if other modules finish faster.
Length is a function of readiness, not the calendar. If fully signed off by Day 14, deploy on Day 15. If a module needs more time, training extends. RH, Manisha and Saurabh decide jointly.

Where Modules 10 and 11 fit (proposed). The framework schedules above predate the process guidelines, so the two administration modules run as afternoon sessions without extending the program: Module 10 alongside Stream 1 (fast track Day 2–3, standard Day 3–5) and Module 11 alongside Stream 2 (fast track Day 6–8, standard Day 10–14). Both must be signed off before the Final Test. RH, Manisha and Saurabh confirm the slots.
What runs every training day, regardless of module
From Day 1, the trainee shadows Jaspreet's full BM day (see "The BM operating day" below). She attends the morning huddles, the BM-Doctor meeting, the 6 PM counsellor debrief and the team close, and fills a practice BM Daily Log each evening. By the Final Test she has seen the full day at least 10 times.
Day 0 · Foundations: what the role is
The BM owns the whole branch, revenue and operations together: "Run the branch as if it were yours. Grow it. Hold it to standard. Build a team that does not need you to run it well."
Session plan (Day 1 morning, 90 minutes, with Harman)
Harman hands over the Founder's letter, the KRA/KPI SOP and this module. The trainee reads the letter in the room (15 min).
Walk through the role purpose, the three jobs and the reporting structure (30 min).
Discuss the Founder's expectations, one by one (30 min).
Fill the Trainee Details block in the Training Tracker: name, assigned clinic, join date, start date, track, expected completion (15 min).
Owner, not supervisor
A BM at GLEUHR is the owner of a clinic, not its supervisor. Most BMs in the industry see themselves as either a sales manager who tolerates operations or an operations manager who supports sales. Neither works:
Strong sales with weak operations: the branch starts losing clients within six months.
Strong operations with weak sales: the branch never grows.
If the trainee comes from a company where these were split, she unlearns that now.
The three jobs (Playbook)
Hold the standard. Clinical, operational and commercial, every day, with or without you on site. You keep the standard; you do not execute it yourself.
Hold the team. Eight to twelve people. Notice them, develop them, defend them, correct them privately, praise them specifically, retain them.
Hold the brand. When something goes wrong, the patient asks for you. When a complaint reaches HQ, it should already be on your desk.
The boss trap
BMs are often promoted for being excellent in a previous role: the best counsellor, the best operations person, the best biller. The instinct is to keep doing that job from a new chair. The real job is to make every person better at their own role than they would be without you.
The inner stance (re-read every morning)
You are not the supervisor of this branch. You are the leader it reaches toward. Hold the standard, hold the team, hold the brand, in that order. The branch should run as well at 3 pm on your day off as at 11 am when you are in your chair.
The model to picture: the most respected school principal you ever knew. Steady, warm, visibly competent. Praise specific and rare enough to be cherished; correction private and kind; trusted by everyone, feared by no one.

The peer relationship with the doctor
The senior doctor leads clinical. The BM leads everything else. Neither reports to the other. They meet daily as equals running parallel functions, and the minutes go to the Regional Head, Manisha and Dr Kanikta (Head of Clinical). Branches where the BM manages the doctor, or the doctor manages the BM, quietly fall apart. Module 4 trains this in depth.

Module 1 · Reception Operations
Stream 1 · Operations · Trainer: Jaspreet (Chandigarh BM) · Fast track Day 1–2 · Standard Day 1–2 · Target 4/4
Why it matters. Reception is the patient's first and last impression of GLEUHR, and the CRM entries made there feed every sales number the BM is judged on.
Learning outcomes
Audit the reception team against the 10-item scorecard.
Run the 5-minute reception morning huddle.
Coach a receptionist on a specific gap in under 10 minutes.
Spot CRM hygiene issues: missing entries, mistagged leads, missed callbacks.
Lesson 1.1 · The receptionist's day (what "standard" looks like)
Time
What must happen
8:45–9:30 Pre-opening
Desk wiped and arranged, water glass set. Appointment list marked: new, returning, VIP, complaint follow-up. Phone log checked, after-hours enquiries answered. Waiting area and washroom checked with housekeeping. Brief with FDM.
9:30–1:00 Morning
Every walk-in: look up, smile, stand briefly, "Welcome to GLEUHR". Patient's name used at least twice. Returning patients greeted with last-visit recall. Every call answered within 3 rings. Every enquiry logged: name, number, concern, follow-up date. Anyone waiting over 10 min acknowledged: "Thank you for your patience". Water offered before asked.
1:00–4:00 Mid-day
Hourly visual check of waiting area. Flow issues to FDM. Payments processed cleanly; never quote without doctor or counsellor handoff. Patient in front always comes before the phone.
4:00–7:30 Afternoon
Goodbye for every departing patient: "Call us anytime, for anything". Walk to the door where possible. Next appointment confirmed in writing (SMS / WhatsApp). Aftercare summary sent. Anyone who left without rebooking flagged to FDM.
7:30–8:00 End of day
Bookings reconciled with attendance. No-shows and cancellations to FDM. Tomorrow's list set up. After-hours messages acknowledged. Desk cleared. EOD note to FDM.
The receptionist's never list: never eat at the desk; no personal phone use at the desk; no gossip within earshot of the waiting area; never discuss one patient's case in front of another; never let a complaint be witnessed openly; never let a patient leave through a door you could have opened; never skip the goodbye.

Lesson 1.3 · The reception morning huddle (5 minutes)
Four items, in this order: yesterday's score, today's appointments, VIPs, risks. Stand, keep it to five minutes, end warm. Use it to praise one specific thing from yesterday by name.
Lesson 1.4 · Coaching a receptionist in under 10 minutes
Coach privately, between patients, never at the desk in front of others. A simple structure:
Name the one gap, with the specific moment you saw ("At 11:20, the caller waited six rings").
Ask what got in the way. Listen.
Show the standard: say or model the exact words or action.
Have her practise it once, right there.
Agree when you will look again, and praise it when you see it held.
Lesson 1.5 · CRM hygiene
What to look for in yesterday's records: enquiries with no entry, leads tagged to the wrong source or stage, callbacks due and not made, follow-up dates missing, no-shows not recorded.

Day 2: Independent scorecard exercise. Score the team, compare with Jaspreet's score, discuss every difference.

Module 2 · Housekeeping & Hygiene
Stream 1 · Operations · Trainers: Arshpreet (Compliance Lead) + Saurabh · Fast track Day 1–2 · Standard Day 3–4 · Target 4/4
Why it matters. In aesthetic medicine, hygiene is both a clinical safeguard and the patient's silent judgement of the brand. Housekeeping holds a standard no one acknowledges; the BM must see it, check it and thank it.
Learning outcomes
Audit housekeeping end to end against the 6-item wall poster standard.
Run the housekeeping morning huddle in Hindi, in the right register.
Coach the housekeeping team without triggering fear or withdrawal.
Explain Saurabh's compliance framework and how it ties to branch audit scores.
Lesson 2.1 · The housekeeping day
Time
Standard
8:00–9:30 Pre-opening
Full walk-through of every area. Windows opened briefly. Every touch surface wiped: door handles, counter edges, magazine covers, switches, chair arms. Washroom deep clean. Every cabin: fresh linen, trolley wiped, floor spotless, drawers organised. Pantry stocked and clean.
Hourly, 10 AM–7 PM
Washroom check, initialled with time: tissue, soap, mirror, floor dry, dustbin under 1/3, gentle fragrance. Waiting area: cushions squared, current-month magazines, glass wiped, dustbin emptied if half full, water topped up, floor swept, plants dust-free.
Between every patient
Cabin reset: linen stripped straight to basket (gloves on); bed, headrest, trolley and side table wiped; floor swept; disposables replaced; dustbin emptied if over 1/3; fragrance refreshed; two-second test at the door.
7:30–9:00 End of day
Deep clean of every cabin. Linen counted, bagged, sent to laundry; fresh linen stacked. Waiting area, washroom, doctor's and counsellor's rooms, reception and pantry reset. Bio-hazard waste sealed and staged. Sharps bin checked and capped if full. 5-minute closing audit with FDM.
The two-second test. Stand at the cabin door and look at it as the next patient will. If anything would catch her eye, it is not ready.
Escalate immediately: needle-stick injury or chemical exposure (stop work, inform FDM / doctor); any patient complaint overheard (say only "I'll call the manager right now"); hazardous spillage (spill kit, inform FDM); a cabin dirtier than a reset can fix (inform FDM before the next patient).
Never: enter a cabin without knocking or while a patient is changing; carry used linen openly through patient areas; handle sharps bare-handed; mix cleaning chemicals; use a phone in patient-facing areas; gossip about a patient.
Lesson 2.2 · The 6-item wall poster standard
The official poster is not in the attached documents. Until Arshpreet supplies it, audit against this working draft drawn from the Housekeeping checklist:
Touch surfaces wiped at opening.
Washroom hourly check done and initialled, every hour 10 AM to 7 PM.
Cabin reset between every patient, passing the two-second test.
Waiting area hourly reset.
Linen, bio-hazard and sharps handled per protocol.
End-of-day deep clean and closing audit with FDM.
Lesson 2.3 · The housekeeping huddle, in Hindi
Five minutes, before opening: today's standards, yesterday's asks and what happened to them, and the cleanliness photo schedule the FDM posts to the team group. Speak Hindi in the team's own register: plain, respectful, warm. Thank one person by name for something specific. Never lecture.
Lesson 2.4 · Coaching without fear
Housekeeping staff often withdraw when corrected by a manager. Correct privately and quietly, show rather than tell, fix the system before blaming the person (Is the spill kit stocked? Is the linen basket in the right place?), and always pair a correction with genuine acknowledgement of what is going well.
Lesson 2.5 · The compliance link (60 minutes with Saurabh)
The BM is measured monthly on the branch compliance audit score (Saurabh + RH), hygiene and protocol adherence (Saurabh + Dr Kanikta) and the housekeeping audit score (BM + Arshpreet). Saurabh walks the trainee through his compliance framework and how a housekeeping miss becomes an audit finding.

Day 2: Independent hygiene audit; compare findings with Arshpreet's.
Day 2: Observe a housekeeping huddle in Hindi, then run one.
Day 2: 60 minutes with Saurabh on the compliance framework.

Module 3 · Therapist Coordination
Stream 1 · Operations · Trainers: Senior Therapist + Jaspreet · Fast track Day 3 · Standard Day 5 · Target 4/4
Why it matters. The cabin is where the patient is most vulnerable, eyes closed, trusting the therapist completely. Therapists report clinically to the doctor; the BM audits the operational standard of delivery and plans workload with the doctor as a peer.
Learning outcomes
Audit treatment delivery: cabin prep, machine handling, timer discipline, handoff.
Spot therapists rushing sessions, skipping protocols or giving an inconsistent experience.
Explain and enforce the three operational rules: timer, verbal handoff, cabin log.
Coordinate therapist workload with the senior doctor.
Lesson 3.1 · The three operational rules
Rule
What the BM checks
Timer
Every session runs to its set time; no rushing to catch up a delayed schedule
Verbal handoff
Patient is handed to the counsellor or reception with a spoken brief, never left to find her way
Cabin log
Every session recorded in the cabin log; case notes complete in the patient file by end of day
Lesson 3.2 · What a correct session looks like (per patient)
Procedures list read and doctor sign-off verified for each one before the shift. Any unsigned procedure is escalated before it starts.
Knock before entering. Wash hands visibly, in the patient's line of sight, every time.
Confirm identity and procedure aloud. Brief in plain language.
Give the stop word: "If at any moment you want me to stop, just say stop."
Cover dignity: sheet, blanket, hair clip with permission. Warm hands, announce the first touch.
Check temperature, pressure and comfort within the first minute. Narrate as you go. Read jaw, breath, fists and feet and adjust before she asks.
End slowly; sit her up before standing. Aftercare in writing (3 points max) sent to her phone before she leaves.
Walk her out or hand off to counsellor / reception.
Then a 3–7 minute cabin reset, and at end of day: deep clean, sharps and bio-hazard disposal per protocol, equipment shutdown per manufacturer protocol, case notes complete, tomorrow's sign-offs verified, EOD note to doctor and FDM.
Lesson 3.3 · Red flags the BM watches for
A session ending early, or a timer reset mid-session.
Hands not washed in sight; stop word not given; no aftercare sent.
A procedure without doctor sign-off, done "as a favour" or under pressure.
Phone in the cabin; talk between colleagues while the patient's eyes are closed.
A session pushed through a clinical reaction instead of stopped.
Clinical escalation (therapist stops and calls the doctor immediately): rash, hives or unusual redness; swelling, especially around eyes or lips; dizziness or faintness; difficulty breathing or chest tightness; burning that does not match the procedure; anything not seen before; anything the gut says is wrong. The BM never decides these; the doctor does.
Lesson 3.4 · Workload planning with the doctor
Therapist scheduling is planned with the senior doctor as a peer. The BM brings the operational view (bookings, cabin availability, wait times, therapist fatigue); the doctor brings the clinical view (which procedures need which therapist, sign-offs, cautions). Agree it; neither overrides the other.

Day 2: Cabin audit walk with Arshpreet.
Day 2: Workload-scheduling exercise with Jaspreet: build tomorrow's therapist schedule from the booking list and agree it with the doctor.
Spot-check exercise: observe sessions and list every protocol miss.

Module 4 · Doctor Coordination: the Peer Relationship (critical)
Stream 1 · Operations · Trainers: Dr Kanikta + Senior Doctor (Chandigarh) + Jaspreet · Fast track Day 4–5 · Standard Day 6–9 · Target 6/6
Why it matters. This is the relationship most BMs in the industry get wrong. A BM who cannot hold a peer relationship with the doctor will damage the branch within months, however good her operations are. Spend the time here even if other modules finish faster.
Learning outcomes
Run the daily BM-Doctor meeting independently.
Draft the MoM the same day, get the doctor's agreement, file it to corporate.
Tell clinical (escalate to the doctor) from operational (handle as BM) without hesitation.
Hold the peer line: neither manage the doctor nor be managed by her.
Lesson 4.1 · The peer line
"We run this branch together. Clinical is yours; operational is mine. The patient gets the best of both." (First affirmation, said or held in mind at every morning meeting.)
Managing the doctor (wrong)
Being managed by the doctor (wrong)
Peer (right)
Telling her how long consults should take
Taking orders on scheduling, staffing or pricing
Agreeing the day's flagged patients together
Pushing her to recommend packages
Letting clinical seniority settle operational calls
Each brings one ask, each owns one action
Overriding a clinical caution to save revenue
Hiding operational problems to avoid friction
Unresolved disagreement goes to the RH, not around her
Lesson 4.2 · The daily meeting (every working day, no exceptions)
Held at 10:05 AM, straight after the huddles, in a 20-minute slot kept free in the doctor’s diary. Open with yesterday in two sentences, then cover the six agenda items from the SOP:
Target review: where the branch stands on revenue and clinical delivery this week.
Client challenges: specific clients with issues, complications, complaints, concerns. Name today's patients who need both leaders' attention ("Mrs Mehta is in at 3; she was wavering on her package; the counsellor will need your weight in the room").
Operational issues: anything in the branch blocking clinical work (consumables, maintenance, cabin availability, wait times).
Clinical issues: anything from clinical that affects operations (therapist sign-offs, cautions, reactions).
Growth plan progress: what is working, what needs to change.
One thing each: one ask the BM has of the doctor, one ask the doctor has of the BM. Include the standard each is holding the other to this week.
The FDM feeds operational inputs into this meeting: wait times, cabin audit findings, complaints. Read them before you walk in.
Lesson 4.3 · The MoM: same-day rule
Drafted by the BM, reviewed by the doctor, agreed in writing.
Filed the same day to the Regional Head, Manisha and Dr Kanikta.
Short: six headings, one per agenda item, one action per item with owner and date.
Recorded in the BM Daily Log column "Doctor MoM filed (Y/N + to RH / Manisha / Kanikta)".
Without the MoM the meeting is a chat. With it, the meeting is a contract. Anything not written down the same day did not happen.
MoM template

Target review: [status] → Action: [what] · Owner: [BM/Dr] · By: [date]2. Client challenges: [names + issue] → Action · Owner · By3. Operational issues: [issue] → Action · Owner · By4. Clinical issues: [issue] → Action · Owner · By5. Growth plan progress: [what is working / changing] → Action · Owner · By6. One thing each: BM asks [..] · Doctor asks [..]Agreed by: Dr [name] (written OK, time)Filed to: RH, Manisha, Dr Kanikta at [time]
Lesson 4.4 · Know the doctor's day
The doctor's own checklist: read the appointment list and returning-patient files; sign off pending therapist procedures; morning meeting with BM; brief the counsellor on key cases; consult room ready (analyser, photo folder, water, screen turned away). In each consult she delivers three affirmations ("Aap theek ho jaayenge"), narrates the skin analysis, frames three findings positively, walks a plan in three stages max, documents in front of the patient and gives the counsellor a handoff brief. At day end she signs off tomorrow's procedures, completes notes, escalates concerns to Dr Kanikta and sends an EOD note to the BM. The BM protects this rhythm; she does not direct it.
Lesson 4.5 · The boundary exercise (10 scenarios)
For each, the trainee says "clinical" or "operational" and what she does. Suggested answers are for Dr Kanikta to confirm or correct.
#
Scenario
Suggested answer
1
A patient asks reception if she can have laser the day after her peel
Clinical. Route to the doctor; reception and BM give no answer.
2
Cabin 2's AC fails mid-morning
Operational. BM re-routes bookings and gets it repaired; informs doctor in passing.
3
A counsellor wants to add a treatment the doctor did not recommend
Clinical. Not allowed; only the doctor recommends treatment. BM corrects the counsellor.
4
The doctor is running 40 minutes late and patients are waiting
Operational flow. BM / FDM inform patients honestly and manage waits; do not rush the doctor's consults.
5
A patient calls two days after treatment with swelling
Clinical. Doctor calls her back the same day. BM documents it and reports to HQ the same day.
6
A therapist wants to do a procedure without sign-off because the doctor is busy
Clinical. Not allowed under any pressure. BM stops it and gets the doctor's decision.
7
A patient with a mild reaction asks for a refund
Both, in order: doctor assesses clinically first; refund is the BM's commercial decision within threshold, above it to HQ.

Module 5 · Counsellor Verification
Stream 2 · Sales · Trainers: Senior Counsellor + Jaspreet + Manisha · Fast track Day 6–7 (with M6) · Standard Day 10–12 · Target 5/5
Why it matters. Counsellors carry the branch's revenue, and the brand's honesty with it. The BM verifies that every rupee is earned the GLEUHR way: honest expectations, no pressure, every follow-up real.

Lesson 5.1 · What a good consultation looks like
The Counsellor Playbook (6 steps) is not in the attached documents. Verify against this flow from the Counsellor daily checklist until it is supplied:
Receive the handover. Greet warmly: "Doctor has shared everything with me, you don't have to repeat anything." Recap the doctor's findings in 60 seconds and mirror to confirm.
Walk the plan. Three stages maximum. Recommend only what the doctor recommended.
Set honest expectations. Timeline, results, what is realistic. No outcome guarantees.
Present the investment. Say "investment", not "price". Offer two options (package and session-by-session; full, EMI or per session). Sit with the silence after the number.
Handle objections as real questions. Read discomfort and adjust. If hesitant: "There is no wrong answer today."
Close cleanly. Yes: hand off to reception for payment and walk her out. No or thinking: written summary in hand, soft-hold a slot, "Whatever you decide, I'm here." Record outcome and reason in the daily tracker.
Before patients arrive the desk is clear: no visible calculator, no price sheet on screen, no number visible from where the patient sits.
The counsellor's never list: no closing techniques (urgency, scarcity, fake offers); no price by phone before consultation; never recommend a treatment the doctor did not; never message a patient at night; never accept off-system payment; never let a hesitant yes become a signature without slowing her down; never argue an objection, answer it.
Escalate to the BM the same hour: any off-system payment request (cash off-books, personal UPI, anything); any refund request (counsellor does not commit); any clinical doubt (back to the doctor immediately); any mention of social media, reviews or legal action; a patient committing beyond her means (slow her down).

Look for: promises in the notes that the doctor did not make; results or timelines stated as certain; follow-up dates missing or passed; hesitations with no follow-up planned; payment terms not recorded; conversion logged without a matching bill.
Lesson 5.4 · Telephony audit
Pull one day's call data and match it to the follow-up list. A real follow-up connected, lasted long enough for a conversation, and has an outcome noted in CRM. A dialled-and-dropped call rang briefly or not at all, was not retried, and is still logged as "followed up". Count both; discuss the gap with the counsellor.

Lesson 8.2 · The development conversation (Playbook)
Most of the time the right answer is develop, not replace. Almost no one came into this work to be bad at it.
In private. Closed-door office, never the corridor.
Specific. Three concrete examples from the last two weeks, not "you have been off".
Curious before corrective. "Help me understand what has been happening for you." The answer may be health, family or feeling passed over.
Co-author the path. "Here is what I will do to support you. Here is what I ask of you over the next four weeks. We sit again in two weeks."
Write it down. A one-page note, signed together, as a shared commitment, not a threat.
Tell HR / HQ briefly. They should not be surprised later.
Coach, escalate or exit
Coach when the gap is skill, knowledge or a temporary situation, and the person engages.
Escalate to the RH when the gap persists after a documented plan, or involves conduct, attendance patterns, harassment, allegations or resignation. Hiring and termination always need RH sign-off.
Exit only after a real development effort. If the person is surprised, the development step was skipped. Never let someone leave thinking she never had a chance.
Never protect a failing team member out of personal loyalty, and never have favourites.

Agree one concrete change each will make. Write it down. Revisit in two weeks.
Never pick sides publicly, even when one side is more right.
The manager who picks sides creates a faction. The manager who avoids conflict creates a toxic peace. The manager who facilitates the hard conversation creates a team.

Lab 1 · The first half-hour (9:30 to 10:05 AM)
Arrive at 9:30 as the clinic opens and walk the branch as a patient would; note 3–5 items for the FDM or housekeeping and 1 thing to praise publicly. Read yesterday's numbers properly (footfall, conversion, walk-ins, complaints, callbacks owed); if the FDM's debrief is missing, ask why before the 9:45 huddles. Mark today's names that matter: VIPs, returning complaints, a fifth-session patient who may be drifting, a new referral. Check the roster and the HQ inbox (Saurabh, Manisha, Tejinder, Dr Kanikta, Urminder sir) and acknowledge briefly once the doctor meeting is done (10:25). Plan the day in three buckets: patient-facing time first, team time, paperwork last.
Avoid: starting in the inbox or on a call; walking into the huddle still on yesterday's problem. The team reads your morning in the first ninety seconds.
Lab 2 · The branch walk (twice a day, 20 minutes)
Mid-morning and late afternoon. Look at reception, waiting area, washroom, corridor, cabins between patients, the doctor's room, the counsellor's room (no number visible from the patient's seat) and team energy. Walk slowly, visibly, warmly; greet every staff member by name.
The FDM walks for compliance (is the standard held in detail). The BM walks for direction (is it the right standard, is the patient experience what we want, is the team in shape). Do not duplicate her walk.
Lab 3 · The personal greeting
Choose deliberately: fifth-plus visit patients, VIPs, anyone returning after a complaint (non-negotiable), patients who travelled from outside the city, special occasions.
"[Name]ji, what a pleasure to see you again. I just wanted to come and say a personal hello. Doctor mentioned your last session went beautifully. If anything at all needs my attention, please ask the desk to find me directly."
Lab 4 · The escalated complaint (10 steps, in this order)
Take the FDM's 20-second corridor brief.
Stand when she walks in; introduce yourself by name and role, warmly.
Sit at her level, beside her rather than behind a desk.
Open with appreciation: "Thank you for telling us this."
Listen fully. Do not interrupt, defend or fill silences.
Acknowledge specifically: "What I am hearing is…" and ask her to correct you.
Apologise without litigating: "That should not have happened to you. I am sorry." Never "I'm sorry you feel that way."
Take responsibility by name: "This is on me, not on the counsellor."
Resolve concretely, without her having to demand it: a fresh consult with the doctor today, a complimentary session, a refund where right, a manager-handled next visit.
Commit to a callback with a timeline, document within the hour (file, complaint log, email to FDM and doctor, Saurabh / HQ if material), then make the call. The follow-through is the real apology.
Never blame a team member by name in front of the patient ("the counsellor will be spoken to" is fine). Never promise what you have not decided to deliver.
Lab 5 · Refund or dispute
Balance what is right for the patient, for the business, and for the precedent. If a refund is right, give it cleanly, warmly and fast. If not (services rendered, package used, a change of mind), say so with respect and offer a real alternative, such as freezing remaining sessions for six months or passing them to a family member. Above the policy threshold, escalate to HQ; never stretch it yourself. Speed is a form of respect: a slow refund reads as resistance.
Lab 6 · The patient who wants to escalate to HQ
"Please do, you absolutely should if it would help. Urminder sir reads patient escalations himself. I will also be writing to them today with everything we have done so far."
Then write to Saurabh, Manisha and your reporting line the same day: facts, what you did, what is next, your assessment. No spin. If you made a mistake, name it.
Lab 7 · Deciding under pressure: the three-question filter
Is this clinical? Then the doctor decides; enable her to decide fast.
Is this a brand question? If the wrong call damages the brand more than doing the right thing costs, do the right thing, fast.
Is it within my authority and reversible? Decide, document, move. If irreversible or outside authority, escalate within the hour.
When you do not know, say so: "Give me ten minutes; I will be back with an answer." An honest pause beats a wrong decision.
Lab 8 · The end-of-day close and the handover
At 6:45 PM, the last fifteen minutes of your shift: stand with the team, name 2–3 specifics by person, acknowledge anything hard, close warmly. Then, before 7:00 PM: send the WhatsApp summary, leave the FDM a handover note for the rest of the day, and plan tomorrow's first half-hour. Callbacks and any note to HQ are done in the 6:15 block; the FDM's debrief is read at 9:30 the next morning.
